Abstract

Modern life increasingly requires participation in more and more digital systems. This correlating with an all-time peak in high-profile data breaches, leaves citizens and their privacy uniquely vulnerable. However, the biggest threat to citizen privacy may not be bad actors, but local law enforcement. The proliferation of digital surveillance devices in police departments throughout the U.S. combined with a lack of oversight and concerning commitment to secrecy, poses a serious risk to the privacy of the American citizen. The Boston Police Department is one of many police departments that has a troubling history with its use of digital surveillance devices; being reprimanded for surveilling parties unrelated to cases, signing a non-disclosure agreement with the FBI obscuring where and when these devices are deployed, and the misutilization of resources sanctioned for counter-terrorism on non-violent drug cases. While programs do exist to identify or remotely shut down these surveillance devices, they remain outdated and unpopular . I plan to bring these detection softwares up to date to provide those who are at elevated risk of unwarranted police surveillance with a tool to defend their privacy, and to use this software to create a live data visualization of any surveillance devices active in Boston.

Background

Introduction

Since the first personal computer became available in 1975 the vast web of human interaction has been migrating from the physical world to the emerging digital one. In 2003 MySpace introduced the masses to social media and accelerated our transition to a world of 1’s and 0’s to lightspeed. So much of our lives are contained within the internet from our friendships to our economic transactions, to the entertainment we consume; you can form a near complete understanding of a person's life just by observing their digital footprint. This comes with inherent risks. 

The threats of online surveillance and data theft grow more prevalent every year. In the last four years, there have been 167 high-profile data breaches exposing hundreds of millions of Americans to bad actors every year. However, not all of the threats to your data are criminal. Both the FBI and local U.S. law enforcement have legal ways to surveil their citizens, the ethics of which have long been a source of controversy. Specifically, the invention of technology like the Stingray and Nyxcell V800, combined with the veil of secrecy surrounding the government's use of surveillance has raised important questions about government oversight, the right to privacy, and the ethics of policing.

Understanding StingRays and Other IMSI-Catchers

Developed by Joachim Frick and Rainer Bott, the “method for identifying a mobile phone user or for eavesdropping on outgoing calls” received its patent from the European Patent Office in November of the year 2000. The telecom industry would later dub this design the IMSI-Catcher, and when the Harris Corporation began manufacturing a similar device in the United States, they called theirs the StingRay. IMSI-Catchers, as the name would imply, are tools for extracting the IMSI (international mobile subscriber identity) from the radio waves sent between mobile phones and cell towers. They do this by masquerading as a legitimate cell tower which tricks mobile phones within a certain radius into sending data to the IMSI-Catcher, then the IMSI-Catcher’s onboard software catalogs the data, before sending it off to a real cell tower to make it appear that nothing out of the ordinary happened. The titular IMSI is the identification number that cell service providers attach to each SIM and eSIM card. Cell service providers use this number as a method of keeping track of customs and their cell plans however, other interested parties have used IMSI numbers, and by extension IMSI-Catchers, in less scrupulous ways.

Because your SIM or eSim card handles all communication between your mobile phone and the rest of the world, controlling it comes with quite a bit of power. For example, hacker communities have long been building virtual base transceiver stations, devices nearly identical to IMSI-Catchers which are used to send any data that utilizes your IMSI number(text messages, files, sometimes even phone calls) to cell towers without paying for a cell service provider. More antagonistic groups use IMSI-Catchers offensively, scraping massive amounts of people's data and then combing through to find either pieces that can be sold to data brokers, or incriminating facts that can used to blackmail the unlucky individual. Both of these uses of IMSI data are illegal with punishments up to and including felony prosecution. Many have levied criticism against the U.S. government’s restrictions on radio wave frequencies citing infringements on personal freedoms and the unfair practice of selling certain frequencies to corporations, thus blocking civilian access. These criticisms are emboldened by the fact that U.S. law enforcement regularly ignores these restrictions to conduct surveillance on civilians. 

Proliferation of Surveillance Technology in American Law Enforcement

American law enforcement is no stranger to surveillance. While the word “wiretapping” and pictures of police officers with headphones on, listening to the conversations of criminals may dominate the image of early police surveillance, in reality, it was quite rare. Even after a 1928 Supreme Court ruling narrowly affirmed the constitutionality of police wiretapping, it was far less popular than the more analog approach of simply observing a person of interest covertly. While the public did rave about the dangers of wiretappers for hire (or private ears, as they were known), it wasn’t until the mid-1950s that law enforcement started to see the value. The FBI of the 50s and 60s had three main targets: Communists, the Mafia, and black people. And FBI director at the time J. Edgar Hoover was convinced that surveillance would be a key weapon in their fight. For example, the FBI’s objective as it pertained to the 1960s civil rights movement, according to an FBI memo, was to “expose, disrupt, misdirect, discredit, or otherwise neutralize” what they called “Black Extremists” or “Black Nationalist Hate Groups”. The unique goal of discreditation combined with the fact that the actions of these unfairly categorized "hate groups" were often not illegal, made surveillance and misinformation campaigns a very viable alternative to arrests (though they were often used in tandem). 

These surveillance programs are still partially classified (which will become a theme), but from the files that were declassified, we know that the FBI was using a mix of technological and analog surveillance. This includes but is not limited to infiltrating student unions and gathering compromising information on future civil rights leaders, all the way to wiretapping phones and planting small microphones known as "bugs" in known revolutionary's hotel rooms. The '60s may have been the FBIs first major foray into spying on its citizens but it had paid dividends; at the expense of black political power, countless lives, and a major blow to the fight for civil rights in America. The FBI had seen the power of surveillance, and although much has changed in the world in the last 75 years, the focus on surveilling telecommunication remains just as, if not more, prevalent than in the age of Hoover.

In the contemporary era, the accessibility and power of surveillance technology has increased dramatically. Immediately following the 9/11 attacks the U.S. government passed the USA PATRIOT (Uniting and Strengthening America by Providing Appropriate Tools Required to Intercept and Obstruct Terrorism) Act, which funneled a monumental amount of money into several internal defense agencies such as the Department of Homeland Security, the Department of the Interior, and the FBI. This manifested in the expansion of American cities' CCTV networks, data sharing deals being struck between cell providers and government agencies, and the selling of military equipment to police departments. This wave of militarization became the home front of the War on Terror. Many major U.S. cities made their own counter-terrorism units, then cited those units when applying for military-grade equipment, including StingRays. 48 police departments across the U.S. purchased StingRays from the FBI (who is the only organization contracted to purchase them from the Harris Corporation), each of these police departments signed non-disclosure agreements prohibiting police from disclosing any information about the use of StingRays.  This secrecy has allowed police conduct ranging from suspicious to illegal. It wasn’t until 2016 that Boston Police needed warrants to use these surveillance devices and even then they raise numerous privacy concerns. The very nature of IMSI-Catchers means that they are imprecise tools, which means even if the police have a warrant to spy on an individual, if they turn on a StingRay in a neighborhood the whole neighborhood is being surveilled. With all these threats to privacy at every turn, it makes one ask the question: How are we supposed to protect ourselves from surveillance?

Crocodile Hunter and the History of Resisting Surveillance

As long as there has been government surveillance, there has been those resisting it. The queer liberation, black power, and anti-war movements of the 60s were all deemed dangerous radicals in their day and thus were heavy targets for government surveillance. They each responded in a number of ways. Developing coded language and social signals, prioritising secrecy and concealing their meetings, creating volunteer teams to scott for prying eyes or unmarked police vans; they responded to analog surveillance with analog solutions. However in the digital age we must respond with digital solutions. The swiss hacking group APT-69420 Arson Cats, hijacked tens of thousands of security cameras in California to bring attention to the scale of government surveillance.. The aptly named Wearable Face Protector was developed to shield the identities of those who participated in the latest Hong Kong protests. The BLMPrivacy bot retroactively censored photos of racial justice protests to prevent them from being cataloged in police databases. Young creatives and thinkers have always worked toward securing their right to privacy even if it means acting against the interests of their government. Perhaps most interestingly in the conversation about StingRays is the now outdated software named Crocodile Hunter after the late Steve Erwin. Crocodile Hunter was a program to detect IMSI-Catchers developed by a team of 5 college students, and was successful until it stopped being supported and encryption technology caught up to them. However the frameworks that were defined by Crocodile Hunter could pave the way for a new technology that could revive their mission and become another tool in the privacy conscious civilians tool belt.

Conclusions
- The threats to young people's digital privacy are numerous and growing.
- StingRays are surveillance devices used by the Boston Police Department that can record all data that passes between cell phones and cell towers.
- American Law enforcement has a troubling history with surveillance and has proven that it cannot be trusted without rigorous oversight that, at the moment, does not exist.
- Young people have always found ways to circumvent government surveillance and in the age of StingRays, Crocodile Hunter may hold the blueprints to increase privacy.
